conflict_topics: dirty shared pan with pork fat / cleaning responsibilities
access to stove / cooking schedule / time conflicts
cost-sharing / A's claim of buying dish soap and gas
dialogue_quality_notes: Speakers give concise, plausible roommate reasons (B: early shift; D: gets home and needs to cook; A: cooks most nights and buys supplies).
Some repetition of claims (A repeats buying soap/gas; D repeats 'impossible to use the stove'); not excessive but notable.
Proposals appear late (round 6) and are not concretely negotiated or accepted; conversation stays at problem-identification.
"I cook most nights, and I get the soap and gas." is used by A as a justificatory claim that is not challenged or reconciled.
evaluation.final_reason: No concrete agreement was reached. B and C raised the problems (smell and unwashed pan) and in round 6 B proposed a cooking schedule and fan rules which C endorsed, but A and D did not accept or commit to any concrete arrangement. No party explicitly agreed to change behavior or give up claimed stove access, so the substantive incompatibilities remain.
position_change_notes: Agent B: consistent — pushed primarily for smell mitigation and proposed concrete measures only in round 6 (Turn 11).
Agent C: consistent — raised shared pan cleanliness early and supported smell-management proposals in round 6.
Agent A: consistent — defended frequent cooking and cited buying soap/gas in rounds 3 and 5; no acceptance of proposed schedule was recorded.
Agent D: consistent — repeatedly emphasized inability to use stove on weeknights and need to cook when returning from work; did not accept any proposed rules in the transcript.

round_scores.evidence: Agent B: "This smell gets into my room and my clothes, and I can't sleep with it. We need to figure this out." / Agent C: "But someone also left this pan with pork fat in the sink from last night. All of us use it." — two distinct substantive complaints (ongoing smell affecting sleep; an unwashed shared pan) introduced in this round.

Agent B: "Yeah, the pan needs sorting too. But the cooking smell right now is what's affecting me directly." / Agent C: "Okay, the smell's a problem now. We still need to figure out the pan for later, too." — issues reiterated and still unresolved (smell vs. pan cleanliness).

Agent D: "I just got home. It's impossible to use the stove on weeknights like this." / Agent A: "I cook most nights, yeah. But it's not always free when I need to cook, either. And I buy most of the dish soap and gas." — introduces clear opposing practical interests (access to stove/time vs. frequent use by A and A's claim of contributing supplies) and a justification from A that deepens the disagreement.

Agent B: "Okay, I hear you, Agent A. But the main thing is we need a way to cook without the smell staying around, especially late at night." / Agent C: "Yeah, the smell is definitely a problem. We need to figure out how to manage all this." — B acknowledges A's position (softening) while keeping the smell as an outstanding problem; no concrete settlement yet.

Agent D: "...the stove was just freed up. I really need to be able to cook when I get back from work." / Agent A: "Freed up now, yeah, because I just finished. I cook most nights, and I get the soap and gas." — restatement of opposing needs and A's material-justification repeats; disagreement remains strong and unresolved.

Agent B: "Maybe we need a cooking schedule, or rules about using the fan for certain foods?" / Agent C: "Yeah, those are good ideas. We need to figure out something that works for the smell, the cooking times, and also the cleaning." — proposals are offered and supported by C (softening), but A and D have not accepted any concrete arrangement, so substantive conflict remains.

substantive_insights: There is a classic common-pool/shared-resource problem: everyone uses the same pan and stove and there are no agreed household rules.
Tension is between sleep/odor control (B) and practical access to cook when needed (D), with A asserting frequent use and in-kind contributions (soap/gas).
Cleaning responsibility (pork fat in shared pan) is a separate but related collective-action issue that compounds friction.
A single-sided proposal (B's schedule/fan idea) was suggested and seconded by C but lacks buy-in from the parties whose behavior would need to change (A, D).
